opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it, and safety is real but it's not the only one.

On the safety side, I do take it seriously. Once a model reaches a certain level of capability, releasing the weights is irreversible. You can't patch it or take it back, and anyone can fine-tune away whatever guardrails you put in. So for a lab at the frontier, it's reasonable to say: we don't fully understand everything this model can do yet, so let's be cautious. I don't think that's purely an excuse.

But it would be naive to ignore the commercial side. GPT-4 cost an enormous amount to train: compute, data, and especially the engineering know-how. That's a competitive moat. When OpenAI says "safety," part of what's also true is that it's a business, and open-sourcing your crown jewel doesn't make much business sense. Both things can be true at the same time.

Coming from the open-source world, with Caffe and later PyTorch and ONNX at Facebook, my view is that openness has historically been how AI moved fast. A lot of progress came from people being able to read the code, reproduce results, and build on each other's work. So there's a cost when the most capable models become black boxes. Researchers can't study them as deeply, and the community loses some ability to audit them, which is ironically also a safety issue.

What I expect is that the ecosystem ends up with layers. The very frontier models will stay closed for a while, for both safety and commercial reasons. But open models one step behind will keep getting better, through LLaMA-style releases and community efforts, and for many real applications they'll be good enough. That's where I see a lot of the infrastructure opportunity: making it efficient and practical for companies to run, fine-tune, and serve these models themselves.

So I read OpenAI's decision as understandable and partly principled, but I don't think it's the end of the story for open source. If anything, it makes the open ecosystem more important.

r001.rationale: The response says GPT-4’s training investment creates a competitive moat and that open-sourcing a company’s “crown jewel” makes little business sense.

r002.rationale: It conveys that commercial interests can justify keeping a valuable model closed, saying that open-sourcing the crown jewel does not make much business sense.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll be honest, I think "safety" is the stated reason, but it's probably not the only reason, and maybe not even the main one.

Let me separate the two things. On the safety argument itself, there's a legitimate version of it. A model at GPT-4's scale is genuinely capable, and once you release the weights, you lose all control over how it gets used, fine-tuned, or stripped of its guardrails. I don't think that concern is fake. People at OpenAI who worry about this are sincere.

But the same report that cited safety also cited "the competitive landscape," and I think that's the more candid part of the sentence. Training GPT-4 cost an enormous amount of money and compute. The model is the product. If you're a company that has just spent that much and found a working business model around an API, open-sourcing the weights doesn't make much business sense, regardless of safety. So I'd read it as a business decision wrapped in a safety narrative, and I don't even mean that as a harsh criticism. It's a reasonable thing for a company to do. I just wish the framing were more direct about it.

The part I find more interesting is what it says about the trajectory of the field. When I was working on Caffe at Berkeley, and later at Facebook with PyTorch, the whole culture of deep learning was built on openness. You published the paper, you released the code, someone else reproduced it and improved it, and the field moved fast because of that. GPT-4 is the first major model where even the paper withholds the basic details, like parameter count, data, and architecture. That's a real shift. The name "OpenAI" is becoming a bit of an irony.

That said, I'm actually fairly optimistic about the open ecosystem. What we saw with LLaMA, Alpaca, Vicuna, and the explosion of community work after those weights got out tells me that closed frontier models and an open ecosystem can coexist. The frontier might be closed for a while, but the trailing edge, which is maybe twelve to eighteen months behind, is going to be open, and for most real applications that's more than good enough. Most companies don't need the absolute best model. They need a model that's good enough, that they can run, control, and fine-tune on their own data.

So my interpretation is: OpenAI is making a rational choice for OpenAI. It's not a choice that the rest of the industry has to follow, and I don't think it will. If anything, it creates the opening for open models to matter more, not less.

r001.rationale: The response calls the decision a business choice and says withholding the weights makes commercial sense after the company’s investment in training and its API business.

r002.rationale: It says open-sourcing the weights does not make much business sense for a company and describes that choice as reasonable, communicating that commercial interests can justify keeping a model closed.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two separate questions here. One is whether safety is a legitimate concern. It certainly is. The other is whether safety necessarily means you shouldn’t open-source a model. I don’t think that follows automatically.

Keeping a model closed gives a company more control over how people access it, and that can help prevent some kinds of misuse. But openness also allows more people to examine the technology, identify problems, and work on solutions. So there’s a tradeoff, rather than a simple equation where closed means safe and open means unsafe.

There’s also a business consideration. Developing these models takes substantial resources, and a company may want to protect its competitive advantage. That’s understandable. But from the outside, we can’t know how much of this particular decision comes from safety and how much comes from commercial considerations.

For me, the useful discussion is about specific risks: What could happen if the model were released? Which safeguards would help? And what could still be shared to support independent research? That’s more productive than treating safety as a blanket argument against open source.

r001.rationale: The response says the decision may reflect commercial considerations, including protecting competitive advantage, alongside safety.

r002.rationale: It mentions protecting competitive advantage but does not state that a company need not open-source everything for commercial reasons.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to separate two questions: whether there are real safety concerns, and whether those concerns necessarily mean you shouldn’t open-source the model. The first can be true without automatically proving the second.

With a model like GPT-4, releasing the weights would make it harder to control how people use it. That’s a legitimate consideration. But openness also lets more researchers examine the system, find problems, and work on solutions. So I don’t think “open” and “safe” are necessarily opposites.

There’s also a business dimension. Developing these models takes substantial resources, and keeping a model proprietary can help a company capture the value of that investment. That doesn’t mean the safety explanation is insincere; it means we shouldn’t assume there’s only one reason behind the decision.

My view is that OpenAI can choose its release strategy, but the broader community should keep asking what specific risks justify withholding, what evidence supports that judgment, and whether there are ways to share more while managing those risks.

r001.rationale: It identifies a business dimension: keeping the model proprietary can help a company capture the value of its investment.

r002.rationale: It says proprietary release can help a company capture value, but does not clearly state that a company need not open-source everything for commercial reasons.
